content.title: About
content.content: Port du Salut is a semi‑soft French cheese with an orange‑red rind, produced from cow’s milk in the Auvergne region. It has a creamy texture, a mild nutty‑butter flavor, and a distinctive aroma that deepens with aging.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese is named after the Port du Salut monastery where it was first made in the 19th century.
The characteristic orange rind is created by adding a natural paprika‑derived coloring.
Often called the “monk’s cheese” because it was originally crafted by Benedictine monks.
The original recipe used only whole whey, but modern versions add cream for a smoother mouthfeel.
Port du Salut is typically served in small wedges to highlight its aroma.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: The cheese is rich in calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Cow’s milk provides complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic bacteria
items.content: During ripening beneficial bacteria develop, contributing to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Low lactose content
items.content: Most lactose is drained with the whey, making the cheese often tolerable for people with mild lactose intolerance.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to casein or whey may react to the cheese.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Port du Salut contains a notable amount of salt; those with hypertension should limit intake.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Like most cheeses, it is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Biogenic amines
items.content: Extended aging can lead to histamine and tyramine formation, which may trigger reactions in sensitive people.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Port du Salut can be enjoyed on its own, sliced thin for sandwiches, added to salads, casseroles, and pasta dishes. It melts well, making it suitable for fondue and baked recipes.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cheese in its original packaging or wrapped in parchment paper inside an airtight container in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C. For longer storage, re‑wrap in wax paper to prevent drying. It keeps best for 4‑6 weeks.
